title: Migrations and Flipper Tag Recoveries of Green Turtles (Chelonia mydas) From Raine Island
content:
ABSTRACT

Studying the movement patterns of marine species enables the creation of targeted management plans, particularly for species like green turtles (Chelonia mydas), whose life cycles are dominated by repeated large-scale migrations. Whereas green turtles undertake numerous migrations throughout their reproductive lives, the postnesting migration routes of nesting turtles from the northern Great Barrier Reef (nGBR) remain relatively undocumented. This study aims to explore these routes using satellite telemetry data from 42 turtles following nesting at Raine Island, a main rookery within the nGBR, and to compare their foraging locations with those obtained from flipper-tag recapture data (n = 747) accumulated over 50 years. The flipper tag recovery data indicate that the geographic range of the northern GBR green turtles spans from Vanuatu to eastern Indonesia and includes most of the north-eastern and southern coasts of Australia and Papua New Guinea, respectively. Satellite tracking of postnesting turtles did not expand the geographic range established by flipper-tag recoveries; however, it provided detailed information on migration routes and corridors. Three key foraging regions were identified, congruent with existing mark-recapture and genetic studies. Two major migration corridors were evident: the first off Cape York in the Torres Strait and the second along a string of reefs between Raine Island and Cape Melville in the Great Barrier Reef. Of these, the corridor off the tip of Cape York spans only ~20 km across at its widest point, and conservative estimates suggest it would have thousands of turtles migrating through annually making it an important route for turtles from the nGBR. This study fills a critical gap in our understanding of green turtle migration routes, offering insights into region-specific management needs and informing conservation strategies to mitigate anthropogenic threats in key migration corridors.
